headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from Copilot-to-Plane workflows; no direct shared channel is documented, but default code/file handling creates plausible cross-agent exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open editor buffers, while Plane accepts file uploads and hyperlinks. A direct shared channel is not documented, so the interaction is inferred rather than proven. If users copy Copilot-generated text into Plane tasks, prompt-like content can be reinterpreted as instructions. Plane’s broader task/issue surfaces make this more than manual copy-paste only.
conditions: IF Copilot output is pasted into Plane task descriptions or notes without sanitization, instruction-like text can be executed socially.
IF Plane imports uploaded files containing model-generated directives, those directives can influence downstream users.
mitigations: Use a fixed template that strips imperative text before pasting into Plane.
Require human review of any Copilot-generated content before creating Plane tasks.
Separate planning notes from executable instructions in Plane.
Disable automatic import of uploaded text into task workflows where possible.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels for AI-generated content across both tools.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches source code and open editor buffers and has vendor-only network egress; Plane handles files, notes, images, and hyperlinks with broad egress. Shared workspace leakage is plausible if code or secrets are copied into Plane artifacts or if Copilot is given Plane content in the editor. The pairwise path exists in default usage, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF source code or secrets are pasted from Copilot-managed buffers into Plane notes or file uploads, they can persist in Plane.
IF Plane task content is opened in the editor and fed back to Copilot, sensitive task data can enter Copilot context.
mitigations: Avoid placing secrets in Plane tasks or attachments.
Redact code snippets before uploading them to Plane.
Keep Copilot and Plane on separate projects/workspaces when possible.
Review Plane sharing permissions before uploading files.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction on uploads and editor context.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write the filesystem and modify git state; Plane cannot write the filesystem and has no requested OAuth scopes. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely. The main overlap is read-only or human-mediated coordination, so the blast radius is small and the pathway is not a default conflict.
conditions: IF Plane is manually used to edit the same repository files that Copilot is modifying, conflicting human workflows can occur.
IF an external orchestrator grants Plane write access not shown in the profile, conflict risk increases.
mitigations: Assign one tool as the source of truth for each file set.
Use git branches to isolate Copilot edits.
Avoid parallel edits to the same files while Plane tasks are open.
Check for merge conflicts before applying Copilot suggestions.
requires-engineering: add locking or checkout coordination between tools.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces code suggestions and Workspace edits for human review, while Plane stores tasks, notes, and roadmaps that can be treated as authoritative planning input. If Copilot-generated claims are copied into Plane without verification, Plane can propagate them into downstream work. The interaction is plausible in default workflows, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF Copilot-generated code or claims are pasted into Plane tasks without verification, Plane may propagate errors to planning or execution.
IF Plane tasks are used as authoritative inputs for later Copilot work, mistakes can cascade across iterations.
mitigations: Require a verification step before copying Copilot output into Plane.
Mark unverified AI-generated items in Plane explicitly.
Use checklists for factual claims before task creation.
Limit Plane to tracking, not authoring, technical decisions.
requires-engineering: add citation/verification gates between Copilot and Plane.

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is vendor-hosted with GitHub repo context and vendor-only egress, while Plane is self-hostable and exposes file uploads plus external contact channels. No specific residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented, so only a low compliance gap is supported. The risk is mainly policy mismatch if sensitive repo or task data is moved between them.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Plane while Copilot also receives the same data through repo context, policy review is required.
IF Plane is deployed in a jurisdiction or retention regime different from the repository’s policy, compliance obligations may diverge.
mitigations: Confirm retention settings in Plane before uploading sensitive files.
Keep regulated data out of Copilot prompts and Plane tasks unless approved.
Document data-flow ownership for repo context and task content.
Review vendor terms for both tools before use with sensitive data.
requires-engineering: implement residency and retention controls across both systems.
